messages.subject: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
parts:
Hello lavaan community, 

I got a bit issue with running CFA in Lavan. There are thousands of videos and blog posts out there to explain the cutoff points and criteria but there are not so many explanations about the case our model doesn't have the perfect indices.  

Well, I want to validate an existing English questionnaire in my country, Iran. For the CFA part, I am facing some issues. 

Well, the questionnaire is a single factor containing 17 items and has been used in different studies in America. Studies indicate that both 17-factor versions and shorter versions (like a brief 4-item version) are valid and reliable. I tried different models like Robust Maximum Likelihood (MLR) and Diagonally Weighted Least Squares (DWLS)). The thing is that the 17-item does not have satisfactory indices in my study (RMSEA is high and CFI and TLI are around 0.8-0.85) and I don't know how I can justify that or address the issue. 

Here are the codes: 
NGS.model.17 <- ' NGranS  =~ NGS1 + NGS2 + NGS3 + NGS4 + NGS5 + NGS6 + NGS7 + NGS8 + NGS9 + NGS10 + NGS11 + NGS12 + NGS13 + NGS14 + NGS15 + NGS16 '
fit17Lik <- cfa(NGS.model.17, data= data, ordered= c("NGS1", "NGS2", "NGS3","NGS4","NGS5", "NGS6", "NGS7","NGS8","NGS9", "NGS10", "NGS11", "NGS12", "NGS13", "NGS14", "NGS15", "NGS16"))
summary(fit17Lik, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
parts: Due to the low factor loading for items 13 and 5, I eliminated the items and reran the model, the results are still not satisfactory.

Model fit is about reproducing the observed (co)variances (or polychoric correlations), not reliability.  You can have a perfectly fitting model with low loadings (so low reliability), or highly reliable indicators yet a misspecified factor structure (so poor fit).  They are mostly independent issues, although the same misspecification will look worse for reliable than unreliable indicators.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Sara,

17 items are many items. Some aspects may be different in Iran. Chances are that you may fix it with a second-order CFA. Item response theory (IRT) may help to form "subscales".

Xavier

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
parts: Do you suggest any way to find a better model fit?

You have to be willing to consider that the theory is wrong or insufficiently complex, at least in the context in which these data were gathered.  As Xavier noted, the items might function differently across cultures, but there have also been instances of mistranslation or inequality of meaning across languages.  

Empirically, you can see which specific pairwise relationships the model fails to reproduce closely.  Use lavResiduals() to inspect the matrix of standardized residuals, and read the reference(s) listed there to understand how to interpret them.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
parts:
Do you suggest any way to find a better model fit? 

You have to be willing to consider that the theory is wrong or insufficiently complex, at least in the context in which these data were gathered.  As Xavier noted, the items might function differently across cultures, but there have also been instances of mistranslation or inequality of meaning across languages.  

Empirically, you can see which specific pairwise relationships the model fails to reproduce closely.  Use lavResiduals() to inspect the matrix of standardized residuals, and read the reference(s) listed there to understand how to interpret them.

Thanks Terrence, 
Should the covariances be less than 0.1 to be accepted as satisfactory results?  

Bests, 
Sara

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting and dealing with nonsignificant results of CFA
parts: Should the covariances be less than 0.1 to be accepted as satisfactory results?

I have never seen a larger criterion, but I have seen smaller.  Usually people are satisfied when their model-implied (co)variances are within 0.05 or 0.10  SDs of their observed (co)variances.  If your model perfectly reproduces variances (typical when residual variances are unconstrained), it should be equivalent to requesting correlation residuals

lavResiduals(fit, type = "cor")

So you could think perhaps more intuitively about whether your model-implied correlations are within 0.05 or 0.10 of observed correlations. 

The point is that mediocre model fit is the accumulation of all the ways your predictions differ from your observations.  Those can include a (few) major misspecification(s), or it could reflect many minor misspecifications.  It is up to you to decide how large of a deviation from observations would be important to address.  The practice of SEM is notorious for lacking objective criteria for making such judgements because they must be based on the substantive domain in which the research is conducted.  There is no magic number that is a good or bad criterion.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
